intro: An average rate of change is the slope of a secant line. Here the secants are drawn over equal intervals, side by side, each in its own color, with its slope beside it and as a bar below the graph. When the bars grow, the rate of change is increasing and the graph is concave up; when they shrink, it is concave down. In Estimate, use one secant line to estimate a value and see whether the estimate lands over or under the curve, and why.
howItWorks:
• Average rate of change of $f$ on $[a, b]$: $\frac{f(b) - f(a)}{b - a}$, the slope of the secant line through $(a, f(a))$ and $(b, f(b))$, in output units per input unit.
  • Equal intervals. Compare rates only over intervals of the same length. If they increase from each interval to the next, the rate of change of $f$ is increasing and $f$ is concave up there; if they decrease, concave down. Constant rates mean a line.
  • Estimate with a secant line: use a point on that line, $f(a) + m(x - a)$, with $m$ the slope.
  • Over or under: on an interval where $f$ is concave up, the graph lies below the secant line, so the estimate is too big (an overestimate); concave down, it lies above and the estimate is an underestimate. Whether $f$ goes up or down does not decide it.
  • Keyboard: the points on the graph take the arrow keys (Shift for bigger steps).
